raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic syndrome in which contrast traverses angiographically normal or near-normal epicardial coronary arteries abnormally slowly. First described by Tambe et al. in 1972 [1], it became more reproducibly characterized after the TIMI frame count was introduced as an objective measure of coronary flow [2]. Most contemporary studies define CSFP by corrected TIMI frame count above approximately 27 frames after excluding obstructive stenosis, coronary ectasia, spasm, embolism, no-reflow after intervention, severe valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, and technical artifacts. Early biopsy and clinical series suggested that CSFP is not merely a visual curiosity: affected patients had microvascular wall thickening, endothelial edema, myocyte ultrastructural abnormalities, recurrent angina, and ischemia-like presentations despite patent epicardial vessels [3,4]. Beltrame and colleagues framed CSFP as a primary coronary microvascular disorder [5] and showed increased resting microvascular tone, reduced coronary sinus oxygen saturation, blunted endothelial responses, and persistence on serial angiography [6,7].

Epidemiologically, CSFP is uncommon but not rare in catheterization laboratories. Reported prevalence varies with population, definition, and referral indication, ranging from approximately 1% to 7% among diagnostic angiograms, and is enriched among patients investigated for acute coronary syndrome or angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries [13,23,30]. Patients are often middle-aged men, smokers, and individuals with hypertension, dyslipidemia, higher body mass index, metabolic syndrome features, or inflammatory/hematologic abnormalities [13,21-24]. However, the phenotype is heterogeneous, and slow flow may involve one, several, or all major coronary arteries; multivessel involvement may reflect a more diffuse disorder [13].

Pathogenesis remains unsettled. The leading model is microvascular dysfunction with both structural and functional components: increased resting resistance, microvascular spasm, impaired nitric-oxide-mediated dilation, and endothelial injury [5,6,8-11,27]. Peripheral endothelial dysfunction and lower nitric oxide levels support a systemic vascular component [8,9]. Homocysteine-related oxidative stress has been associated with impaired flow-mediated dilation [10], and newer translational work links slow-flow states to oxidative metabolism, thioredoxin-interacting protein signaling, and vascular inflammation [28]. Perfusion studies have been mixed: nuclear imaging and hemodynamic investigations support inducible ischemia in some patients [6,12], whereas invasive physiologic studies suggest that angiographic slow flow is an imperfect surrogate for coronary microvascular dysfunction because it reflects resting contrast transit rather than hyperemic reserve [11,25,26]. This distinction is clinically important: CSFP may overlap with INOCA, microvascular angina, or vasomotor disorders, but should not automatically be equated with any single endotype.

Clinical presentation is dominated by recurrent chest pain, often at rest, with abnormal stress tests or acute coronary syndrome–like presentations [4,13,23,30]. Most patients have preserved systolic function, but recurrent symptoms can drive repeat emergency visits and angiography. Serious events are uncommon but reported, including myocardial infarction without obstructive coronary disease, ventricular arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death [15]. These observations justify careful risk-factor assessment and follow-up rather than reassurance that the angiogram is simply “normal.”

Diagnosis requires a disciplined angiographic approach. Operators should use standardized acquisition, adequate contrast injection, and quantitative frame counting where possible [2,13,24]. Secondary causes must be excluded before labeling “primary” CSFP. When symptoms persist or ischemia is documented, coronary function testing with adenosine and acetylcholine can clarify whether there is impaired coronary flow reserve, high microvascular resistance, epicardial spasm, or microvascular spasm [25-27]. Non-invasive tests may demonstrate ischemia, but normal perfusion does not exclude episodic microvascular spasm or endothelial dysfunction [12].

Management is empirical because randomized trials are small. Lifestyle intervention and aggressive treatment of hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, insulin resistance, and inflammation are reasonable given frequent cardiometabolic clustering [13,21,23,24,29]. Calcium-channel blockade has the most consistent mechanistic rationale. Mibefradil improved frame counts and angina in early crossover data [17], and diltiazem improved symptoms and exercise parameters in a randomized trial [16]. Nicorandil improved acute angiographic flow and, in a randomized comparison, relieved angina better than nitroglycerin [18,19]. Nebivolol improved endothelial function and chest pain in observational interventional studies, possibly through nitric-oxide-mediated effects [20]. Antiplatelet or anti-inflammatory strategies remain investigational, although platelet activation indices and inflammatory markers correlate with CSFP in several cohorts [21,22,29]. Overall, CSFP should be viewed as a measurable angiographic sign with heterogeneous mechanisms, frequent symptom burden, and uncertain prognosis; future trials should combine standardized frame-count definitions with invasive coronary function endotyping and patient-centered outcomes.
